analysis.one_liner: Requires EPA to set enforceable national drinking water limits for PFAS 'forever chemicals' within two years.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote; it sat in committee for the rest of the 117th Congress and died there.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS are man-made 'forever chemicals' used in nonstick cookware, weatherproof clothing, and firefighting foam; they persist in the environment and have been linked to health harms. The bill would have amended the Safe Drinking Water Act to require EPA, within two years, to publish a health goal and set a national legal limit for total PFAS in public drinking water, with the limit set to protect people at elevated risk. It was introduced in May 2021 with 11 Democratic cosponsors, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its environment subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of people who drink public water contaminated with PFAS, including communities near military bases, industrial sites, and airports where firefighting foam has been used. A national enforceable limit would require water systems to test for PFAS and treat or replace contaminated sources, and would give residents a legal standard to hold suppliers accountable.

how_it_helps.text: Requires EPA to publish a maximum contaminant level goal and promulgate a national primary drinking water regulation for total PFAS within two years of enactment [S2][S3].
Requires the limit to be protective of subpopulations at greater risk of harm from PFAS exposure, such as children and pregnant women, rather than the general population alone [S2][S3].
Sets these limits in statute with a hard deadline, instead of leaving the timing to EPA's discretion, after years in which PFAS remained unregulated in drinking water [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Water utilities, which would have to test and install treatment to meet a national PFAS limit, with compliance costs likely passed through to customers in water bills; manufacturers that make or use PFAS, who would face tighter regulation and greater liability exposure.

drawbacks.text: A two-year statutory deadline is fast by drinking-water-rule standards; setting a limit before the underlying health and treatment science is fully settled risks a number that is hard to defend or hard to meet [S3].
Compliance costs would fall on water systems first and be passed to ratepayers through water bills, hitting customers of small systems with contaminated wells and limited rate bases the hardest.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large: an enforceable national limit on chemicals in drinking water that millions of people cannot avoid consuming. The costs are genuine but ordinary for a drinking water standard — testing and treatment paid for through utility rates — and the bill's health-protective framing for vulnerable groups reflects how EPA normally sets such goals. The main design weakness is the aggressive two-year deadline, which was the point of the bill but left little room for a careful rulemaking.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its environment subcommittee in May 2021, and no markup, hearing, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brendan F. Boyle (D-PA) introduced the bill on May 17, 2021, joined by 10 cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S4][S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce on May 17, 2021, and to the Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change the next day [S5].
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers and water utilities were spared a statutory deadline to set and meet drinking water limits; households on contaminated water got no enforceable federal standard from Congress, though EPA later set the first national PFAS drinking water limits in 2024 under its existing authority.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican support appears in the record; no vote was ever taken, so opposition showed up as committee inaction rather than a roll call [S4][S5].

industries.note: A statutory national drinking water limit for PFAS would have tightened regulation of the chemicals these firms make and increased their liability exposure, including in contamination lawsuits. Their interest was in avoiding or delaying such a mandate, while residents of contaminated communities want the opposite.

Utilities would bear the cost of monitoring and treatment to meet a national PFAS limit, costs typically passed to ratepayers, but they would gain a single clear federal standard and, where water is currently contaminated, their customers would gain enforceable protection.

industries.industry: Consumer product makers (nonstick cookware, weatherproof clothing, firefighting foam)
industries.note: The bill regulated drinking water rather than the products themselves, so the direct cost was limited, but an enforceable water standard increases the pressure, legal and regulatory, on the products that put PFAS into the environment in the first place [S2].
